explanation: D-amino acid oxidase (D-AA oxidase flavoprotein) is the FAD-dependent enzyme responsible for oxidative deamination of D-amino acids and glycine, converting them to corresponding alpha-keto acids and ammonia.
D-AA oxidase flavoprotein converts D-amino acids to alpha-keto acids by removing the amino group, eliminating the asymmetry of the alpha-carbon atom and producing a racemic mixture with L-forms.

Transdeamination of glutamine involves glutamine transaminase (producing glutamate and alpha-keto glutaramate) followed by omega-amidase, ultimately yielding alpha-ketoglutarate as the carbon skeleton product.

Glutamate dehydrogenase catalyzes the reversible oxidative deamination of glutamate to alpha-ketoglutarate, producing ammonia and NAD(P)H; this is the key reaction linking amino acid metabolism with TCA cycle.
L-glutamate dehydrogenase is the major pathway for oxidative deamination of amino acids in mammals, converting L-glutamate to alpha-ketoglutarate with production of ammonia and NAD(P)H.
keyConcept: L-GDH as main oxidative deamination enzyme

explanation: Liver and kidney are the primary organs for oxidative deamination, but heart, brain, and skeletal muscle also carry out this reaction, contributing to amino acid nitrogen disposal.
L-glutamate dehydrogenase requires NAD+ (for oxidative deamination) or NADP+ (for reductive amination) as coenzymes, reflecting its reversible nature in nitrogen metabolism.
True: NAD+ is the coenzyme for oxidative deamination ( glutamate to alpha-ketoglutarate), while NADP+ is used in reductive amination (alpha-ketoglutarate to glutamate), maintaining redox balance.
ADP and GDP (guanosine diphosphate) allosterically stimulate L-glutamate dehydrogenase, increasing ammonia production during energy deficit states when more amino acids need to be catabolized.
ATP, GTP, and NADH allosterically inhibit L-glutamate dehydrogenase, preventing excessive ammonia production when energy status is adequate and reducing glutamate catabolism.
D-amino acid oxidase is a flavoprotein requiring FAD (flavin adenine dinucleotide) as its prosthetic group, which accepts electrons during the oxidative deamination reaction.
D-amino acid oxidase is found primarily in liver and kidney peroxisomes, where it metabolizes D-amino acids from dietary sources and bacterial cell walls.
Deamidases (glutaminase for glutamine, asparaginase for asparagine) are the enzymes responsible for nonoxidative deamination, releasing ammonia directly by hydrolyzing the amide group.
Ketoglutarate-D-AA oxidase flavoprotein acts on D-amino acids and glycine as substrates, performing transdeamination reactions that link amino acid metabolism to TCA cycle intermediates.
In the liver, glutamine is cleaved by glutaminase to produce glutamate and ammonia; the ammonia enters the urea cycle while glutamate enters energy metabolism or gluconeogenesis.
Lysine, threonine, proline, and hydroxyproline cannot undergo transamination because they lack an alpha-amino group or have secondary amino groups that are not recognized by aminotransferases.
Alanine transaminase (ALT) catalyzes the conversion of pyruvate to alanine in muscles, using glutamate as the amino donor; this is part of the glucose-alanine cycle transporting nitrogen to liver.
L-amino acid oxidase catalyzes the oxidative deamination of L-amino acids to corresponding alpha-keto acids, producing hydrogen peroxide and ammonia; FMN is its required cofactor.

Non-oxidative deamination of glutamine and asparagine is catalyzed by specific deamidases (glutaminase, asparaginase), releasing NH3 which enters the urea cycle in liver or is excreted in urine by kidneys.
NH3 released by hepatic deamidases enters the urea cycle in hepatocytes, where it is combined with CO2 and ammonia from other sources to form urea for renal excretion.
NH3 released by renal deamidases is not converted to urea but diffuses into the tubular lumen and is excreted directly in urine as ammonium ion.
Sources of ammonia include amino acid catabolism (transamination, oxidative deamination), purine/pyrimidine catabolism, glutaminase action, amine oxidation, and intestinal bacterial metabolism.
Synthetic fates of ammonia include incorporation into non-essential amino acids via reductive amination (glutamate from alpha-ketoglutarate) and glutamine synthesis via glutamine synthetase.
The major mechanism of ammonia excretion in the liver is urea synthesis via the urea cycle, which converts two molecules of ammonia (one free, one from aspartate) into one urea molecule.

Hepatic encephalopathy is diagnosed by excluding other causes of altered mental status, identifying precipitating factors (infection, bleeding, electrolytes), and observing rapid improvement with ammonia-lowering treatment.

Lactulose treats hepatic encephalopathy by acidifying colonic contents (conversion to lactic/acetic acid), reducing ammonia absorption, and decreasing ammonia-producing bacteria through osmotic catharsis.
Neomycin treats hepatic encephalopathy by killing intestinal bacteria that produce ammonia from protein catabolism, reducing the ammonia load reaching the liver through portal circulation.
Sodium benzoate, sodium phenylbutyrate, and sodium phenylacetate are ammonia scavengers used to increase nitrogen excretion in urea cycle disorders and hepatic encephalopathy.
Sodium benzoate conjugates with glycine to form hippuric acid, which is rapidly excreted in urine, effectively removing one nitrogen atom from the body per molecule of benzoate.
L-ornithine-L-aspartate (LOLA) stimulates the urea cycle by providing substrates (ornithine and aspartate) for carbamoyl phosphate synthetase I, enhancing ammonia fixation and disposal.

Hyperammonia decreases Krebs cycle activity and ATP production, reduces GABA synthesis (causing hyperexcitability), disrupts cerebral electrical activity, causes cerebral edema, and increases serotonin production.

Hyperammonemia causes include acquired forms (liver cirrhosis, hepatitis, portosystemic shunts) and congenital forms (urea cycle enzyme deficiencies, ornithine transporter defects, N-acetylglutamate synthase deficiency).
The first step of the urea cycle is carbamoyl phosphate synthesis from ammonia and CO2, catalyzed by carbamoyl phosphate synthetase I in the mitochondrial matrix, consuming 2 ATP.
Carbamoyl phosphate synthetase I (CPS I) is the enzyme responsible for carbamoyl phosphate synthesis in the first step of the urea cycle, requiring N-acetylglutamate as an obligate activator.
Ornithine transcarbamoylase catalyzes the second step of the urea cycle, transferring the carbamoyl group from carbamoyl phosphate to ornithine, forming citrulline.
The second step of the urea cycle is citrulline synthesis, catalyzed by ornithine transcarbamoylase (OTC), occurring in the mitochondrial matrix.
The third step of the urea cycle is argininosuccinate synthesis, catalyzed by argininosuccinate synthetase, where citrulline combines with aspartate in the cytosol.
The fourth step of the urea cycle is cleavage of argininosuccinate by argininosuccinate lyase to form arginine and fumarate in the cytosol.
The final step of the urea cycle is cleavage of arginine by arginase to form urea and ornithine, with ornithine being transported back to mitochondria to repeat the cycle.
Carbamoyl phosphate synthetase I (CPS I) is the rate-limiting enzyme of the urea cycle, allosterically activated by N-acetylglutamate and subject to substrate availability control.

Urea synthesis occurs exclusively in the liver mitochondria and cytosol, while excretion is performed by the kidneys; the liver synthesizes urea from ammonia and the kidneys filter and excrete it in urine.

The mitochondrial enzyme used in pyrimidine synthesis is carbamoyl phosphate synthetase II (CPS II), distinct from the cytosolic enzyme; the question may refer to amidophosphoribosyltransferase or dihydroorotate dehydrogenase.
